Summary and Beige Book context:
- The FOMC cut the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound (0–0.25%), launched large-scale purchases of Treasuries ($500B+) and agency MBS ($200B+), expanded repo operations, eased the discount window, eliminated reserve requirements, and activated coordinated dollar swap lines to support market functioning and credit flow.
- Beige Book signals show the coronavirus already weighing on activity across Districts: travel and tourism fell sharply; consumer spending moderated; manufacturing faced supply chain disruptions; the energy sector came under stress; and transportation activity was mixed (with isolated port strength but broader headwinds). Labor markets were tight through February but firms reported constraints and growing uncertainty; price pressures were muted and inflation below 2%.
- Credit conditions: loan growth was impacted and banks tightened standards (including for C&I and CRE), raised credit score thresholds, reduced limits, and reported weaker consumer demand, with expectations of further tightening and deterioration in collateral values—consistent with SLOOS and amplifying downside risks.

Implications: Despite aggressive policy support, Beige Book evidence of broad-based demand weakness, supply chain issues, and tightening credit supply suggests transmission to the real economy will be constrained in the near term, leaving the outlook skewed to the downside.
